To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) to detect chromosomal polysomy in Barrett’s esophagitis (BE) tissue specimens can accurately and objectively distinguish between high-grade dysplasias and adenocarcinomas in BE tissue specimens.
FISH is a useful tool for diagnosing HGD and EA in BE specimens.
FISH is able to differentiate between high-grade dysplasias and non-high-grade dysplasians with a sensitivity of about 80% and specificity of 88%.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for the diagnosis of Barrett’s esophagitis, a disease that affects millions of people worldwide.
the development of a new method for the detection of high-grade dysplasias in Barrett's esophagus.
the development of a novel method for detecting high-grade esophageal cancer.

FISH is a useful adjunct in the diagnosis of dysplasia and cancer in BE specimens.
this study provides evidence that FISH may be a useful adjunctive test in the evaluation of dysplastic BE specimens.
the use of FISH in the diagnosis of dysplasia is not recommended at this time, but that further research is needed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FISH analysis can be useful in the diagnosis of dysplasia and adenocarcinomas in patients with BE.
the FISH probe set used in this study is able to differentiate between dysplasia and non-dysplasia in BE with high accuracy.
polysomy by FISH is a good predictor for the presence and grade of dysplasia and can be used to help differentiate between dysplastic and nondysplastic BE.

FISH can be used to identify HGD/EA with a sensitivity of >80% and a high degree of specificity.
